item.description:

  • Experience 2 — Homelidays and the millions of lines of Classic ASP
  • Experience 3 — Visual Studio and the deleted MSI installer projects
  • Experience 4 — The consignment shop and the Windows licence
  • Experience 5 — Windows 7 then Windows 10: imposed waste
  • Experience 6 — Windows Phone: a new phone with every generation
  • Experience 7 — OneDrive and our family photos
  • Experience 8 — Balsamiq and the imprisoned file format
  • Experience 9 — PC Soft: changing the rules mid-game
  • The common thread: who really controls the software?
  • Free software: regaining room to manoeuvre
  • And me, in all this? A path, not a posture
  • Conclusion
  • Sources and references

Why this article#

I spent more than twenty years developing and architecting software. Over those years, I watched the same scenario repeat itself: a technology company decides, alone and unilaterally, to abandon a technology, break compatibility, change a price or a licence — and users, freelancers, associations, whole companies find themselves left high and dry. Not by accident, but because the very model of proprietary software allows it.

item.title: The flip side of permissive licences — FreeBSD, and freedom for whom?
item.description:
• What is a permissive licence?
  • FreeBSD, a complete operating system, free… and permissive
  • How the giants exploit FreeBSD
    • Netflix: the invisible infrastructure
    • Sony PlayStation: the locked fortress
    • Apple: the technological Frankenstein
  • The nuance: what the giants really give back
  • And copyleft?
  • Sources and references

In the founding article of this series, I recounted how proprietary software ends up abandoning its users. The answer I champion is free software. But “free” is not a single block: there are two great families of licences, with opposing philosophies.

item.title: Copyleft licences: the freedom that can't be taken back
item.description:
• What is copyleft?
  • How the GPL came to be
  • Two axes to keep from getting lost
  • The GPL family: LGPL, GPL, AGPL (the “strength” axis)
  • Tivoization and the asymmetry of power
  • Beyond tivoization: the other contributions of GPLv3
  • Two philosophies, one wish
  • Sources and references

The first instalment of this series explored permissive licences (BSD, MIT, Apache) through FreeBSD: they leave everyone free to do what they like with the code, including closing it back up. Here is their counterpart: copyleft licences.

item.title: Why the Linux kernel stayed on GPLv2: Torvalds versus GPLv3
item.description:
• A preliminary point: “GPLv2 only,” not “v2 or later”
  • The core objection: the licence covers the software, not the hardware
  • “Pro-DRM”: what he actually said
  • The real divide: FSF ethics versus open-source pragmatism
  • In short
  • Sources and references

In the previous article on copyleft licences, one detail was worth pausing on properly: GPLv3 (2007) added an anti-tivoization clause, and the Linux kernel never moved to GPLv3. The most visible opponent of that version: Linus Torvalds, the creator of Linux.
